claim: Nuclear exclusion of YAP/TAZ is considered necessary for adult tissue homeostasis.
source: Nuclear exclusion of the transcriptional regulators and potent oncoproteins, YAP/TAZ, is considered necessary for adult tissue homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Nuclear YAP/TAZ are essential regulators of peripheral nerve development and myelin maintenance.
source: Here we show that nuclear YAP/TAZ are essential regulators of peripheral nerve development and myelin maintenance.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study presented in the abstract.

claim: Developing Schwann cells require YAP/TAZ to enter S-phase.
source: To proliferate, developing Schwann cells (SCs) require YAP/TAZ to enter S-phase and, without them, fail to generate sufficient SCs for timely axon sorting.
evidence: This is a finding from the study presented in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: SCs without YAP/TAZ fail to generate sufficient SCs for timely axon sorting.
source: To proliferate, developing Schwann cells (SCs) require YAP/TAZ to enter S-phase and, without them, fail to generate sufficient SCs for timely axon sorting.
evidence: This is a finding from the study presented in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: SCs require YAP/TAZ to upregulate Krox20 for differentiation.
source: To differentiate, SCs require YAP/TAZ to upregulate Krox20 and, without them, completely fail to myelinate, resulting in severe peripheral neuropathy.
evidence: This is a finding from the study presented in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: SCs without YAP/TAZ completely fail to myelinate.
source: To differentiate, SCs require YAP/TAZ to upregulate Krox20 and, without them, completely fail to myelinate, resulting in severe peripheral neuropathy.
evidence: This is a finding from the study presented in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Loss of YAP/TAZ in SCs results in severe peripheral neuropathy.
source: To differentiate, SCs require YAP/TAZ to upregulate Krox20 and, without them, completely fail to myelinate, resulting in severe peripheral neuropathy.
evidence: This is a finding from the study presented in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Nuclear YAP/TAZ are selectively expressed by myelinating SCs in adulthood.
source: Remarkably, in adulthood, nuclear YAP/TAZ are selectively expressed by myelinating SCs, and conditional ablation results in severe peripheral demyelination and mouse death.
evidence: This is a finding from the study presented in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Conditional ablation of YAP/TAZ in adult SCs results in severe peripheral demyelination.
source: Remarkably, in adulthood, nuclear YAP/TAZ are selectively expressed by myelinating SCs, and conditional ablation results in severe peripheral demyelination and mouse death.
evidence: This is a finding from the study presented in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Conditional ablation of YAP/TAZ in adult SCs results in mouse death.
source: Remarkably, in adulthood, nuclear YAP/TAZ are selectively expressed by myelinating SCs, and conditional ablation results in severe peripheral demyelination and mouse death.
evidence: This is a finding from the study presented in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: YAP/TAZ regulate both developmental and adult myelination by driving TEAD1 to activate Krox20.
source: YAP/TAZ regulate both developmental and adult myelination by driving TEAD1 to activate Krox20.
evidence: This is a finding from the study presented in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Krox20 is the master transcription factor that drives myelin gene expression for both myelin formation and maintenance.
source: Krox20 (also called Egr2) has been identified as the master transcription factor that drives myelin gene expression for both myelin formation and maintenance (Topilko et al., 1994; Decker et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: YAP and TAZ are Hippo pathway transcriptional co-activators and potent oncoproteins that shuttle between cytoplasm and nucleus.
source: YAP (Yes-associated protein) and its paralogue, TAZ (Transcriptional coactivator with PDZ-binding motif), are Hippo pathway transcriptional co-activators and potent oncoproteins that shuttle between cytoplasm and nucleus (Hansen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: When activated, YAP/TAZ translocate to the nucleus where they potently induce cell proliferation.
source: When activated, YAP and TAZ (hereafter YAP/TAZ) translocate to the nucleus, where they potently induce cell proliferation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: YAP/TAZ lack DNA binding domains and act indirectly by binding partner transcription factors, particularly members of the TEAD family.
source: Because YAP/TAZ lack DNA binding domains, they act indirectly by binding partner transcription factors, particularly members of the TEA domain (TEAD) family (Zhao et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Following phosphorylation by activated Hippo pathway, YAP/TAZ are inactivated through cytoplasmic retention and ubiquitin-mediated degradation.
source: Following phosphorylation by activated Hippo pathway, YAP/TAZ are inactivated through cytoplasmic retention and ubiquitin-mediated degradation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Nuclear translocation of YAP/TAZ in differentiated adult cells is essential for cancer initiation or growth of most solid tumors.
source: Indeed, nuclear translocation of YAP/TAZ in differentiated adult cells is essential for cancer initiation or growth of most solid tumors (Harvey et al., 2013; Moroishi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: YAP/TAZ are emerging as attractive targets for cancer therapies.
source: Accordingly, YAP/TAZ are emerging as attractive targets for cancer therapies (Zanconato et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: YAP/TAZ are strongly localized in the nuclei of immature SCs at E16.5.
source: Using these antibodies and an antibody for Sox10, a specific marker of the SC nucleus, we confirmed that YAP/TAZ were strongly localized in the nuclei of immature SCs at E16.5 (Figure 1A and E), when SCs are actively proliferating and sorting out large axons (Jessen and Mirsky, 2005).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A and E.

claim: YAP/TAZ continued to be expressed strongly in SC nuclei at P4, P18 and P60.
source: Notably, YAP/TAZ continued to be expressed strongly in SC nuclei at P4, P18 and P60.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by immunostaining data.

claim: Immunostaining of transcriptionally inactive, phosphorylated-YAP (p-YAP) was largely cytoplasmic.
source: Immunostaining of transcriptionally inactive, phosphorylated-YAP (p-YAP) was largely cytoplasmic, as expected, indicating nucleocytoplasmic shuttling of YAP/TAZ in mature SCs (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: YAP was highly expressed in myelinating SCs but virtually undetectable in Krox20-negative, non-myelinating SCs at P60.
source: We therefore co-immunostained P60 teased sciatic nerve fibers for Sox10, Krox20 (to selectively label mSCs) and YAP. Strikingly, YAP was highly expressed in mSCs (Figure 1C; arrows), but virtually undetectable in Krox20-negative, non-myelinating SCs (Figure 1C; eg., arrowheads).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Postnatal Yap/Taz cDKO mice developed severe peripheral neuropathy.
source: Consistent with a recent report (Poitelon et al., 2016), postnatal Yap/Taz cDKO developed severe peripheral neuropathy, whereas neither Yap nor Taz cKO showed an abnormal phenotype.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental observations and consistent with a cited report.

claim: Neither Yap nor Taz single cKO showed an abnormal phenotype.
source: Consistent with a recent report (Poitelon et al., 2016), postnatal Yap/Taz cDKO developed severe peripheral neuropathy, whereas neither Yap nor Taz cKO showed an abnormal phenotype.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental observations.

claim: As early as P7, cDKO mice began to develop tremor, splayed gait and hindlimb paralysis, which progressively worsened with age.
source: As early as P7, cDKO mice began to develop tremor, splayed gait and hindlimb paralysis, which progressively worsened with age (data not shown).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental observations.

claim: By P60 both hindlimbs of cDKO mice were completely paralyzed, and the forelimbs displayed obvious weakness.
source: By P60 both hindlimbs were completely paralyzed, and the forelimbs displayed obvious weakness (Figure 2A, Video 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2A and Video 1.

claim: Sciatic nerves of P60 Yap/Taz cDKO were translucent due to virtually complete absence of myelin.
source: Sciatic nerves of P60 Yap/Taz cDKO were translucent due to virtually complete absence of myelin (Figure 2B), and compound muscle action potentials (CMAPs) were absent in footpad muscles.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Compound muscle action potentials (CMAPs) were absent in footpad muscles of P60 cDKO mice.
source: Sciatic nerves of P60 Yap/Taz cDKO were translucent due to virtually complete absence of myelin (Figure 2B), and compound muscle action potentials (CMAPs) were absent in footpad muscles.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by electrophysiological data.

claim: Spontaneous and irregular potentials occurred in P60 cDKO footpad muscles.
source: Notably, spontaneous and irregular potentials occurred in P60 cDKO footpad muscles (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Myelin basic protein (MBP) was undetectable in P60 cDKO mice, except in rare SCs which retained strong YAP/TAZ immunoreactivity.
source: Cellular analysis confirmed complete amyelination in P60 cDKO mice. In stark contrast to controls, myelin basic protein (MBP) was undetectable (Figure 2E1), except in the rare SCs which retained strong YAP/TAZ immunoreactivity (Figure 2E1 and E, arrows).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2E1 and E.

claim: Many axons were singled out by promyelinating SCs with thick basal lamina in P60 cDKO.
source: Notably, however, although we frequently observed small bundles of unsorted axons, many axons were singled out by promyelinating SCs with thick basal lamina in P60 cDKO (Figure 2F and inset).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Radial sorting is not blocked in Yap/Taz cDKO mice, but proceeds abnormally and remarkably slowly.
source: These results show that radial sorting is not blocked in Yap/Taz cDKO mice, but that it proceeds abnormally and remarkably slowly.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on experimental observations.

claim: SCs lacking YAP/TAZ arrest as promyelinating SCs and are unable to myelinate axons.
source: These results demonstrate that SCs lacking YAP/TAZ arrest as promyelinating SCs (that is, fail to differentiate into mSCs), and are therefore unable to myelinate axons.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on experimental observations.

claim: Myelination appeared completely normal in the sciatic nerves of P60 Yap cKO.
source: In contrast to Yap/Taz cDKO, myelination appeared completely normal in the sciatic nerves of P60 Yap cKO (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B) and nearly so in those of P60 Taz cKO, except for rare small bundles of unsorted axons (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by histological data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Myelination appeared nearly normal in the sciatic nerves of P60 Taz cKO, except for rare small bundles of unsorted axons.
source: In contrast to Yap/Taz cDKO, myelination appeared completely normal in the sciatic nerves of P60 Yap cKO (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B) and nearly so in those of P60 Taz cKO, except for rare small bundles of unsorted axons (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by histological data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: YAP and TAZ are redundant in regulating SC differentiation and myelination.
source: These results show that YAP and TAZ are required for SC differentiation and myelination. They also suggest that YAP/TAZ are redundant in regulating SC differentiation and myelination, and that TAZ is the more potent regulator.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on experimental observations.

claim: TAZ is the more potent regulator of SC differentiation and myelination compared to YAP.
source: These results show that YAP and TAZ are required for SC differentiation and myelination. They also suggest that YAP/TAZ are redundant in regulating SC differentiation and myelination, and that TAZ is the more potent regulator.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on experimental observations.

claim: At P4, cDKO sciatic nerves contained large bundles of unsorted, mixed-caliber axons, whereas many axons were already sorted and myelinating in controls.
source: At P4, cDKO sciatic nerves contained large bundles of unsorted, mixed-caliber axons, whereas many axons were already sorted and myelinating in controls (Figure 3A,P4).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by histological data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: At P18, when myelination appeared complete in control nerves, proximal nerves of cDKO contained many large bundles of unsorted axons.
source: At P18, when myelination appeared complete in control nerves, proximal nerves of cDKO contained many large bundles of unsorted axons (Figure 3A: P18 proximal).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by histological data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Numbers of Sox10+ SCs in cDKO were reduced to half or less of those in control mice from E17.5 to P60.
source: From E17.5 to P60, numbers of Sox10+ SCs in cDKO were reduced to half or less of those in control mice (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B), and Ki67+ proliferating SCs were substantially reduced at P0 (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by quantitative immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Ki67+ proliferating SCs were substantially reduced at P0 in cDKO.
source: From E17.5 to P60, numbers of Sox10+ SCs in cDKO were reduced to half or less of those in control mice (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B), and Ki67+ proliferating SCs were substantially reduced at P0 (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by quantitative immunostaining data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: At E17.5, only ~10% SCs were dividing in Yap/Taz cDKO, compared to ~30% SCs in control mice.
source: At E17.5, when SC proliferation peaks with active axon sorting, only ~10% SCs were dividing in Yap/Taz cDKO, compared to ~30% SCs in control mice (Figure 4C and E), concomitant with the reduced SC numbers in cDKO sciatic nerves (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 4C and E.

claim: Less than 1% of SCs completely lacking YAP/TAZ were EdU+ at P4, whereas ~15% of SCs with residual YAP/TAZ were dividing.
source: We found that less than 1% of SCs completely lacking YAP/TAZ were EdU+, whereas ~15% of SCs with residual YAP/TAZ were dividing (Figure 4D and F).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 4D and F.

claim: YAP/TAZ are required for proper proliferation of immature SCs.
source: Collectively, these results show that YAP/TAZ are required for proper proliferation of immature SCs, and that the subsequent reduction in SCs resulted in the failure of timely axon sorting in cDKO.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on experimental observations.

claim: The reduction in SCs resulted in the failure of timely axon sorting in cDKO.
source: Collectively, these results show that YAP/TAZ are required for proper proliferation of immature SCs, and that the subsequent reduction in SCs resulted in the failure of timely axon sorting in cDKO.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on experimental observations.

claim: Integrin α6 protein and mRNA expression were markedly reduced in P60 cDKO sciatic nerves.
source: Our immunohistochemical analysis revealed no integrin α6 in SCs in P60 cDKO (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A). Western blotting and RT-qPCR analysis of cDKO sciatic nerves also showed markedly reduced protein and mRNA expression of integrin α6 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by immunostaining, Western blotting, and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Radial sorting proceeds, albeit abnormally and remarkably slowly, in the absence of laminin receptors.
source: This result therefore confirms the earlier report of Poitelon et al. that YAP/TAZ regulate the expression of integrin α6 and presumably other laminin receptors. This result also suggests that radial sorting proceeds, albeit abnormally and remarkably slowly, in the absence of laminin receptors.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on experimental observations.

claim: An abnormally high number of cDKO SCs expressed Oct6 from P0 to adulthood.
source: In control nerves, the number of Oct6+ SCs peaked at P4, and then sharply declined. In striking contrast, an abnormally high number of cDKO SCs expressed Oct6 from P0 to adulthood (Figure 5A and C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5A and C.

claim: cDKO SCs failed to upregulate Krox20: ~15% of SCs were Krox20+ throughout development and adulthood in cDKO, compared to ~30% at P0 and ~70% from P18 onwards in control mice.
source: Notably, cDKO SCs failed to upregulate Krox20: in control mice, ~30% of SCs were Krox20+ at P0, increasing to ~70% from P18 onwards, whereas in cDKO, ~15% of SCs were Krox20+ throughout development and adulthood (Figure 5B and D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5B and D.

claim: Krox20 mRNA expression was greatly reduced in cDKO.
source: As expected, Krox20 mRNA expression was also greatly reduced (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: YAP/TAZ initiate SC differentiation and myelination by upregulating Krox20 expression in promyelinating SCs.
source: Together, these results suggest that YAP/TAZ initiate SC differentiation and myelination, presumably by upregulating Krox20 expression in promyelinating SCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on experimental observations.

claim: Within two weeks of the first tamoxifen injection, Yap/Taz iDKO mice displayed persistent shivering, ataxia, hunched posture, weight loss and rapid shallow breathing, which progressively worsened until death within the next two weeks.
source: Within two weeks of the first tamoxifen injection, Yap/Taz iDKO, but not control, mice displayed persistent shivering, ataxia, hunched posture, weight loss and rapid shallow breathing, which progressively worsened until death within the next two weeks (Figure 6A and B, Video 2, n > 8).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 6A and B, and Video 2.

claim: Adult Plp1-creERT2; Yapfl/fl; Tazfl/fl mice exhibited a similar phenotype to Sox10-creERT2 iDKO and died with respiratory failure within one month after the first tamoxifen injection.
source: We found that adult Plp1-creERT2; Yapfl/fl; Tazfl/fl mice exhibited a similar phenotype (eg., Figure 6E) and died with respiratory failure within one month after the first tamoxifen injection.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Nerve conduction velocity (NCV) in iDKO was ~16 m/s, which was markedly reduced from ~50 m/s in control mice.
source: Nerve conduction velocity (NCV) in iDKO was ~16 m/s, which was markedly reduced from ~50 m/s in control mice (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Electron microscopy of iDKO sciatic nerves revealed numerous demyelinating axons.
source: Electron microscopy of iDKO sciatic nerves revealed numerous demyelinating axons (Figure 6E2 and G): some were completely demyelinated (Figure 6E2 and E3; red 'a'), others were undergoing demyelination and showed loosened or disorganized myelin sheaths (Figure 6E2 and E3; yellow 'a').
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 6E2 and G.

claim: Longitudinal sections of iDKO nerves demonstrated segmental demyelination with adjacent myelinated or demyelinated internodes.
source: Longitudinal sections demonstrated an additional striking features of iDKO axons: segmental demyelination with adjacent myelinated or demyelinated internodes (Figure 6E4; demyelinated internodes marked by 'a').
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by histological data shown in Figure 6E4.

claim: Non-myelinating SCs or Remak bundles were unaffected in iDKO.
source: Non-myelinating SCs or Remak bundles were unaffected (data not shown), consistent with the absence of nuclear YAP/TAZ in non-myelinating SCs.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental observations.

claim: Oligodendrocytes in adult WT mice did not express YAP/TAZ.
source: Oligodendrocytes in adult WT mice did not express YAP/TAZ (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), and myelination in the optic nerves in both iDKO mice appeared normal (data not shown).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Myelination in the optic nerves in both iDKO mice appeared normal.
source: Oligodendrocytes in adult WT mice did not express YAP/TAZ (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), and myelination in the optic nerves in both iDKO mice appeared normal (data not shown).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental observations.

claim: Central demyelination cannot account for the iDKO phenotypes.
source: Therefore, central demyelination cannot account for the iDKO phenotypes.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on experimental observations.

claim: Many DAPI+ nuclei in iDKO nerves had only faint Krox20 immunoreactivity, and only occasional nuclei exhibited strong Krox20 immunoreactivity.
source: Notably, immunostaining of iDKO nerves revealed that many DAPI+ nuclei had only faint Krox20 immunoreactivity and, only occasional nuclei exhibited strong Krox20 immunoreactivity (Figure 7A, arrow).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: YAP/TAZ were virtually undetectable in nuclei that stained weakly for Krox20 in iDKO.
source: Moreover, YAP/TAZ were virtually undetectable in nuclei that stained weakly for Krox20 (Figure 7A, arrowheads).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Sox10+ SC nuclei in iDKO mice were frequently labeled faintly or not at all for Krox20.
source: Lastly, Sox10+ SC nuclei in iDKO mice were frequently labeled faintly or not at all for Krox20 (Figure 7B, arrowheads; Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: YAP/TAZ maintain adult myelination of peripheral nerves by promoting Krox20 expression.
source: These results suggest that YAP/TAZ maintain adult myelination of peripheral nerves, presumably by promoting Krox20 expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on experimental observations.

claim: Four potential TEAD binding sites were identified in the Krox20 MSE.
source: Interestingly, we identified four potential TEAD binding sites in the MSE (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1) (Diepenbruck et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only TEAD1 was detectable in YAP/TAZ immunoprecipitates from P12-P15 sciatic nerves.
source: Sox10, YY1, NFAT3, NFAT4 and TEADs 1 and 4 were robustly expressed (Figure 8B and C1). Notably, only TEAD1 was detectable in YAP/TAZ immunoprecipitates (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The direct association of TEAD1 particularly with TAZ was confirmed by counter immunoprecipitation with anti-TEAD1 antibody.
source: The direct association of TEAD1 particularly with TAZ was confirmed by counter immunoprecipitation with anti-TEAD1 antibody (Figure 8C1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 8C1.

claim: TEAD1 is a partner TF of TAZ for developmental myelination.
source: Therefore, TEAD1 is a partner TF of TAZ for developmental myelination.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on experimental observations.

claim: MSE regions encompassing primer sets E3, E4, and E5 showed strong association with TEAD1 in P12-15 sciatic nerves.
source: MSE regions encompassing primer sets E3, E4, and E5 showed strong association with TEAD1 (Figure 8D; >50 fold more binding than control).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: YAP/TAZ-TEAD1 binds to Krox20 MSE to upregulate Krox20 for SC differentiation and myelination.
source: These results suggest that YAP/TAZ-TEAD1 binds to Krox20 MSE, in order to upregulate Krox20 for SC differentiation and myelination, and are consistent with an earlier report (Lopez-Anido et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on experimental observations and consistent with a cited report.

claim: TEAD1 specifically bound to regions encompassing E3, E4 and E5 in P70 sciatic nerves.
source: Notably, TEAD1 specifically bound to regions encompassing E3, E4 and E5 (>50 fold enriched compared to control IgG), as well as the promoter region (>10 fold enriched).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by ChIP-qPCR data.

claim: The MSE is active in adult myelinating SCs.
source: These results are the first to demonstrate that the MSE is active in adult mSCs, and suggest that YAP/TAZ-TEAD1 continues to act on the MSE to drive Krox20 transcription for adult myelination.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on experimental observations.

claim: YAP/TAZ-TEAD1 continues to act on the MSE to drive Krox20 transcription for adult myelination.
source: These results are the first to demonstrate that the MSE is active in adult mSCs, and suggest that YAP/TAZ-TEAD1 continues to act on the MSE to drive Krox20 transcription for adult myelination.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on experimental observations.

claim: TEAD1 was strongly expressed by proliferating, differentiating, and mature SCs.
source: Lastly, we investigated TEAD1 expression in SCs at various stages. TEAD1 was strongly expressed by proliferating, differentiating, and mature SCs (Figure 8F and G; P4 and P18 data not shown), suggesting that YAP/TAZ-TEAD1 drives SC proliferation, differentiation and maintenance.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by Western blotting and immunostaining data shown in Figure 8F and G.

claim: Non-myelinating SCs and cDKO SCs lacking YAP/TAZ also expressed TEAD1.
source: Non-myelinating SCs (data not shown) and cDKO SCs lacking YAP/TAZ (Figure 8H) also expressed TEAD1, suggesting that it is the presence or absence of YAP/TAZ which determines transcriptional regulation of Krox20 by TEAD1.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8H.

claim: It is the presence or absence of YAP/TAZ which determines transcriptional regulation of Krox20 by TEAD1.
source: Non-myelinating SCs (data not shown) and cDKO SCs lacking YAP/TAZ (Figure 8H) also expressed TEAD1, suggesting that it is the presence or absence of YAP/TAZ which determines transcriptional regulation of Krox20 by TEAD1.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on experimental observations.

claim: YAP/TAZ are required for SC proliferation important for timely axon sorting.
source: In this report we identify YAP/TAZ as essential regulators of SC proliferation and myelination. YAP/TAZ are required for 1) SC proliferation important for timely axon sorting, 2) SC differentiation critical for myelination, and 3) maintenance of differentiated myelinating SCs essential for myelin maintenance.
evidence: This is a main conclusion from the study based on experimental observations.

claim: YAP/TAZ are required for SC differentiation critical for myelination.
source: In this report we identify YAP/TAZ as essential regulators of SC proliferation and myelination. YAP/TAZ are required for 1) SC proliferation important for timely axon sorting, 2) SC differentiation critical for myelination, and 3) maintenance of differentiated myelinating SCs essential for myelin maintenance.
evidence: This is a main conclusion from the study based on experimental observations.

claim: YAP/TAZ are required for maintenance of differentiated myelinating SCs essential for myelin maintenance.
source: In this report we identify YAP/TAZ as essential regulators of SC proliferation and myelination. YAP/TAZ are required for 1) SC proliferation important for timely axon sorting, 2) SC differentiation critical for myelination, and 3) maintenance of differentiated myelinating SCs essential for myelin maintenance.
evidence: This is a main conclusion from the study based on experimental observations.

claim: The findings are the first to show that YAP/TAZ can be required for adult tissue homeostasis.
source: Our findings are the first to show that YAP/TAZ can be required for adult tissue homeostasis and suggest caution in targeting them for cancer therapy.
evidence: This is a main conclusion from the study based on experimental observations.

claim: The study suggests caution in targeting YAP/TAZ for cancer therapy.
source: Our findings are the first to show that YAP/TAZ can be required for adult tissue homeostasis and suggest caution in targeting them for cancer therapy.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on experimental observations.

claim: Proliferation of SCs lacking both YAP/TAZ was markedly inhibited due to repressed entry into S-phase.
source: We found that proliferation of SCs lacking both YAP/TAZ was markedly inhibited due to repressed entry into S-phase.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental observations.

claim: The markedly delayed radial sorting in cDKO mice was primarily due to the failure of SCs lacking YAP/TAZ to generate sufficient SCs at the appropriate time.
source: These data therefore strongly suggest that the markedly delayed radial sorting in cDKO mice was primarily due to the failure of SCs lacking YAP/TAZ to generate sufficient SCs at the appropriate time.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on experimental observations.

claim: A YAP/TAZ-TEAD1 complex initiates SC differentiation and myelination by directly binding to the Krox20 MSE.
source: Our evidence therefore strongly suggests that a YAP/TAZ-TEAD1 complex initiates SC differentiation and myelination by directly binding to the Krox20 MSE.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on experimental observations.

claim: Signals in adult myelinating SCs regulate nucleocytoplasmic shuttling of YAP/TAZ to maintain activation of Krox20 via its MSE.
source: Our findings, however, strongly imply that signals in adult mSCs regulate nucleocytoplasmic shuttling of YAP/TAZ to maintain activation of Krox20 via its MSE.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study based on experimental observations.

claim: TEAD1 may actively repress Krox20 transcription in non-myelinating SCs and Yap/Taz cDKO SCs.
source: It is also interesting that non-myelinating SCs and Yap/Taz cDKO SCs express TEAD1, despite absence of YAP/TAZ. TEADs can repress transcription in the absence of YAP/TAZ (Koontz et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2014). It is conceivable, therefore, that TEAD1 actively represses Krox20 transcription in these SCs, consequently maintaining amyelination.
